ai.definition: Cancer genomics involves the application of genomic technologies to study the genetic alterations in cancer cells. It aims to identify specific mutations, amplifications, and deletions that contribute to tumor development and progression.
ai.howItWorks: Advanced sequencing techniques are used to generate a comprehensive map of an individual's cancer genome. This data is then analyzed using bioinformatics tools to identify unique genetic signatures associated with the patient's specific type of cancer. Based on these insights, tailored therapeutic strategies can be developed to target the underlying genetic drivers of the disease.
ai.problemSolved: Cancer genomics addresses the heterogeneity and complexity of cancers by providing a deeper understanding of individual tumors at the molecular level, enabling more precise and effective treatment approaches compared to traditional one-size-fits-all therapies.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process for cancer genomics involves the use of high-throughput sequencing platforms. These platforms require sophisticated equipment such as next-generation sequencers, specialized reagents, and bioinformatics software for data analysis.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes sample collection from patients, DNA/RNA extraction, library preparation, sequencing, and data processing. Each step requires careful quality control to ensure the accuracy of the genetic information obtained.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include the high initial investment in sequencing technology, ongoing maintenance costs for equipment, labor-intensive data analysis processes, and the need for specialized expertise in genomics and bioinformatics.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is positive as more clinical trials demonstrate the efficacy of personalized cancer treatments. However, widespread adoption faces challenges related to cost, regulatory approval, and infrastructure development.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks vary by region but generally require rigorous validation and approval processes for both sequencing technologies and therapeutic applications based on genomic data.
ai.risks: Technical risks include the potential for false positives or negatives in genetic testing. Ethical concerns arise from privacy issues related to handling sensitive patient information and the risk of exacerbating healthcare disparities if not implemented equitably.
ai.profitability: Profitability is variable, with early-stage companies facing significant upfront costs but potentially high returns on investment through successful clinical trials and commercialization of personalized therapies.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving sequencing technologies for faster turnaround times, reducing costs, and integrating genomics data with other omics data (e.g., proteomics) to develop more comprehensive treatment strategies.

glossary.def: Changes in the DNA sequence or structure that can lead to cancer development and progression.
Advanced sequencing technologies capable of generating vast amounts of genetic data quickly and cost-effectively.
The use of computational tools to analyze biological data, including genomic sequences, for research and clinical applications.

subsystems.name: Sample and sequencing lab
subsystems.role: gets usable tumour DNA and RNA from a patient.
parts: blood draw for circulating tumour DNA (liquid biopsy)

subsystems.name: Sequencing platforms
subsystems.role: reads the sequence of the cancer genome.
parts: targeted gene panels (tens to hundreds of genes)

subsystems.name: Bioinformatics pipeline
subsystems.role: turns raw reads into a list of real variants.
parts: read alignment to the reference genome
signatures such as tumour mutational burden and microsatellite instability

subsystems.name: Clinical reporting and records
subsystems.role: delivers a decision to the treating oncologist.

buildSteps.title: Take a sample
buildSteps.detail: A pathologist confirms tumour tissue in a biopsy, or a blood sample is drawn to capture DNA shed by tumours.

buildSteps.title: Extract nucleic acids
buildSteps.detail: DNA and RNA are purified; in formalin-fixed tissue the DNA is often degraded, which limits what can be detected.

buildSteps.title: Prepare a sequencing library
buildSteps.detail: DNA is fragmented, tagged with patient-specific barcodes, and target regions are captured with probes if a panel is being used.

buildSteps.title: Sequence
buildSteps.detail: A high-throughput sequencer reads each fragment many times so that low-level mutations in a mixed sample can be seen.

buildSteps.title: Call and filter variants
buildSteps.detail: Software aligns reads to the reference genome and separates true cancer mutations from sequencing errors and inherited variation.

buildSteps.title: Annotate and interpret
buildSteps.detail: Each variant is matched against databases and drug evidence, and a molecular tumour board weighs it with the patient's clinical picture.

buildSteps.title: Select therapy
buildSteps.detail: The oncologist uses actionable findings to choose a targeted drug, immunotherapy or clinical trial, sometimes with the original diagnosis set aside.

buildSteps.title: Monitor
buildSteps.detail: Repeat blood tests can track whether mutations are shrinking or a resistant clone is emerging.

prerequisites.why: cost per genome has fallen by orders of magnitude since the early 2000s, making tumour sequencing practical.

prerequisites.tech: A finished human reference genome and variant databases
prerequisites.why: interpreting a cancer genome requires knowing what normal human variation looks like.
only a minority of detected variants currently has a matching approved therapy.
assays must be validated and accredited before results can guide treatment.
each genome is tens to hundreds of gigabytes and must be stored and shared under consent rules.

pathway.milestone: targeted panels are routine for several cancers, and some drugs are approved by mutation rather than by organ
pathway.unlocks: better outcomes in lung cancer, melanoma and some colorectal and ovarian cancers, and access to tissue-agnostic therapies.

pathway.milestone: whole-genome and RNA sequencing become affordable enough for routine care
pathway.unlocks: detection of structural rearrangements, fusions and non-coding drivers that panels miss.

pathway.milestone: liquid biopsies used to monitor treatment response and relapse
pathway.unlocks: repeated, non-invasive testing and earlier detection of resistance.

pathway.milestone: blood-based multi-cancer early detection and functional testing of variants in the lab
pathway.unlocks: screening before symptoms and better prediction of which drug will actually work.
